To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cytokine induction renders viral cccDNA vulnerable and allows its specific degradation, which in turn eliminates HBV infection.
cytokine-induced nuclear deamination by host cytidine deamidases, APOB EC3A and A POBE C3B, degrades HBV covalently closed c ircular DNA (cccDNA) and thus prevents HBV r eactivation.
interferon and lymphotoxins induce specific degradation of nuclear hepatitis B virus (HVB) covalently closed-circular DNA (cccDNA) by up-regulating APOBEC family members.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of viral replication and persistence of hepatitis B virus ( HBV ), and with the identification of novel antiviral targets and strategies.
the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of chronic HBV infection, which is a major global health problem.
understanding and controlling the molecular mechanisms that underlie the establishment and maintenance of the HBV cccDNA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the APOBEC family of enzymes can be used as a therapeutic target to treat HBV infection.
APOBEC-mediated degradation of nuclear HBV cccDNA is an important mechanism of antiviral defense that is induced by cytokines, and it may have therapeutic potential.
the APOBEC family proteins are involved in the innate immune response of the host against HBV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nuclear HBV cccDNA can be targeted for degradation by specific APOBEGs (A3A and A3B) that are induced by cytokines.
the APOBEC family of mRNA-editors is a key player in the host defense against hepatitis B virus (see the Perspective by Shomai and Rice).
we have identified the first host factor that specifically targets the nuclear covalently circular DNA (ccc-DNA) and that this factor is a member of the APOBEC family.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have discovered a new mechanism of antiviral activity against HBV.

APOBEC-mediated cytidine de-amination is not a random, nonspecific event but a highly targeted and selective mechanism that is induced in the presence of HBV and can lead to degradation of viral but not host DNA.
we have found a way to eliminate hepatitis B virus from infected hepatocytes without damaging them.
